planting.note: Set bulbs 6-8 inches deep in autumn in rich, sharply drained soil; this Central Asian species is the wild parent behind many taller hybrid onions and needs a hot, dry summer rest to reflower reliably.

directions: Plant bulbs in autumn, 6-8 inches deep, in loose, fast-draining soil amended with grit if heavy; full sun and a baking-dry summer dormancy keep the bulbs healthy for years. In late spring to early summer each bulb sends up a single sturdy scape topped by a loose, airy globe of starry violet-purple flowers that opens from the bottom upward over several weeks. The strappy basal leaves tend to yellow and collapse before the flowers peak, so interplant with later-emerging perennials to mask the foliage. Leave the papery seed heads standing for garden structure into autumn.

planting.note: Plant small bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in any well-drained soil; this Mediterranean species naturalizes readily and also sets aerial bulbils, so site it where some spread is welcome.

directions: Set bulbs 3-4 inches deep in autumn in ordinary, well-drained garden soil in full sun to light shade; rosy garlic tolerates poor, dry ground and needs no fertilizing. Rounded umbels of pale to deep pink, star-shaped flowers open in late spring atop slender stems, often mixed with small bulbils that let the clump expand on its own over the years. Because of this self-propagating habit it can become weedy in mild climates, so deadhead spent umbels where containment matters. The grassy, onion-scented foliage dies back by early summer as the plant goes dormant for the dry season.

planting.note: Plant small bulbs 2-3 inches deep in fall in lean, gritty, sharply drained soil; this western North American wildflower is adapted to winter-wet, bone-dry-summer conditions and resents rich or constantly moist ground.

directions: Site bulbs in fall in a rock garden, gravel bed, or other spot with sharp drainage and full sun; this native of dry slopes from British Columbia to California thrives on winter and spring moisture followed by complete summer drought. In late spring to early summer, wiry stems carry tight umbels of rose-pink to magenta flowers with distinctive pointed, tapering tepals, held just above a few grass-like leaves. The foliage withers soon after bloom as the bulb enters dormancy, so mark the planting location or pair it with later-season companions. Avoid summer irrigation once the plant goes dormant, as excess moisture during the rest period causes bulb rot.

planting.note: Plant small bulbs 2-3 inches deep in fall in a gritty, humus-light rock garden mix; this diminutive Chinese species prefers even moisture during growth rather than a bone-dry summer rest.

directions: Grow in a rock garden, trough, or raised bed with gritty, well-drained but not parched soil in full sun to very light shade. This miniature Yunnan native forms tufts of thread-like, almost needle-fine leaves topped in mid to late summer by small, nodding, bell-shaped flowers of an unusually vivid cobalt to steel blue. Because it stays only a few inches tall, it is easily lost among coarser neighbors, so give it an open spot at the front of a trough or scree bed. Divide congested clumps every few years in early spring to maintain vigorous flowering.

planting.note: Plant bulbs or divisions in fall or early spring in average, well-drained garden soil; this Japanese and Korean species is unusual among ornamental onions for flowering in autumn rather than summer.

directions: Plant in average garden soil with reliable drainage in full sun to light afternoon shade; established clumps tolerate both summer heat and ordinary garden watering better than many drought-dormant alliums. Clusters of narrow, grass-like leaves build through summer and are followed in September and October by dense, rounded umbels of rosy-purple to magenta flowers, a welcome late-season contrast to typical spring and summer bulb bloom. The low mounding habit and tidy foliage make it a good edging plant or rock garden subject rather than a border accent. Clumps slowly increase and can be divided in spring every three to four years to refresh vigor.

planting.note: Plant bulbs or divisions in fall in humus-rich, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil; this Himalayan species grows naturally in damp meadows and appreciates more consistent moisture than most ornamental onions.

directions: Grow in fertile, humus-rich soil that stays evenly moist through the growing season, in full sun to light shade; unlike many drought-dormant alliums, this Himalayan native resents prolonged summer drought. Flat, strap-shaped leaves form loose clumps from which tall, hollow scapes rise in mid to late summer, carrying loose, open umbels of deep reddish-purple to violet star-shaped flowers. It combines well with moisture-loving perennials and grasses in a mixed border rather than a typical dry bulb bed. Established clumps can be divided in early spring to propagate and to keep plantings vigorous.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in gritty, sharply drained soil on a slope or raised bed; this southwestern Alps native of rocky, sun-baked slopes needs excellent drainage to avoid summer rot.

directions: Plant in a sunny rock garden or raised bed with gritty, fast-draining soil; this alpine native of the southwestern Alps is intolerant of winter wet at the crown and performs best on a slope. Wiry stems carry a few nodding, bell-shaped flowers in deep rose to magenta-pink from mid to late summer, each with a faint lily-like flare to the tepals that gives the species its name. The glaucous, grassy foliage is sparse and unobtrusive, leaving the flowers to stand out against surrounding gravel or low companion plants. Established clumps are long-lived but resent disturbance, so leave them undisturbed once settled.

planting.note: Plant small bulbs 2-3 inches deep in fall in gritty, well-drained but not parched soil; this Yunnan species, collected for the Bees of Chester nursery by plant hunter George Forrest, suits a rock garden or raised bed.

directions: Grow in a rock garden or raised bed with gritty, humus-light soil that drains freely but does not bake completely dry, in full sun to light afternoon shade. Narrow, grass-like leaves form small tufts beneath slender stems that carry a handful of nodding, bell-shaped flowers in clear sky blue to violet-blue during late summer, an unusual color among dwarf alliums. The compact size and pendant flowers make it best appreciated at close range in a trough or scree planting rather than a border. Divide crowded clumps in early spring if flowering declines.
